title: Redwood cost economics discovery with Newgate Capital
transcript:
00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I think we've got about 45 minutes, is that still good for folks?
00:08 Liam: Yep that's perfect, thanks Maya.
00:11 Maya: Quick intro: I'm Maya Chen, AE at Redwood, and Daniel my SE is with me to dig into the cost and perf stuff.
00:18 Daniel: Hi all.
00:20 Aisha: Hi, thanks.
00:22 Maya: Quick agenda — talk a bit about current infra and usage, go into per-token pricing and batching/caching levers, hosted vs dedicated vs private cost trade-offs, and agree on a pilot/benchmarks. Sound right?
00:33 Liam: Sounds good.
00:35 Noah: Yep.
00:38 Maya: Great — Liam, can you give us a quick overview of the workload and what success looks like?
00:44 Liam: Sure. So we're building a deal desk assistant that summarizes legal docs and internal memos, plus a model-driven Q&A over our research corpus. Roughly 10k queries/day today, expecting 3x growth next year. Latency target is soft — sub 700ms preferable for interactive internal use, but finance will push on cost per call.
01:05 Noah: Yeah on the cost side we have a budget target of under $X per 1k calls — I'm not going to quote exact number on the call — but we need predictable unit economics.
01:16 Daniel: Got it. When you say queries, are you talking about single-turn prompts or multi-turn chat context?
01:21 Liam: Mostly single-turn summarization and short Q&A; average prompt plus response token payload is around 600 tokens.
01:29 Daniel: OK that's helpful. So two knobs we typically talk about: per-token pricing (hosted) and system-level levers like batching, prefix/KV caching and quantized models which change throughput and unit cost.
01:40 Aisha: How do those levers map to hosted vs dedicated vs private? We care about data residency and keys, plus control over scaling.
01:47 Maya: Great question. High level: Hosted is easiest, pay-per-token, we manage everything. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools — lower unit cost at commit levels, predictable throughput, and better isolation. Private is about VPC or on-prem with control over networking and KMS — it can increase ops overhead and base cost.
02:05 Liam: Can you give a concrete per-token example? Like, what's the delta between hosted and dedicated for a 600-token payload?
02:12 Daniel: Sure, rough numbers: Hosted lists at around $0.03 per 1k input tokens and $0.06 per 1k output tokens for certain model classes — ranges vary by model and quantization. So for 600 tokens (say 200 input / 400 output) that's about — quick math — < $0.03 per call on hosted for some smaller models, but it's model-dependent. With Dedicated, with a commit, you often see 20-50% lower unit cost due to amortizing GPU time and enabling more aggressive batching.
02:41 Noah: Is that with batching enabled by default?
02:43 Daniel: Yes, the runtime does continuous batching. For Dedicated we can tune batch sizes more aggressively because you control capacity and have predictable traffic. Also caching helps: prefix/KV cache for repeated prefixes (e.g., standard prompt template or system instructions) can drop token counts by 10-40% in real workloads.
02:59 Aisha: Do we need to change our model to use caching? Our engineers are using streaming responses and kv-cache is already used in our transformer infra but i'm not sure how it maps.
03:10 Daniel: No code change for the app in most cases — the runtime manages KV cache at serve time. If you do model variants that support persistent KV cache across requests, we save tokens that otherwise re-compute attention states.
03:21 Liam: Are there cases where quantization hurts quality for our summarization?
03:25 Daniel: Short answer: sometimes. For long-form summarization we recommend trying 4-bit or 8-bit quantization profiles that Redwood verifies per-model. We pair that with eval prompts to ensure quality doesn't regress — and you can do canary rollouts.
03:37 Noah: From finance perspective we need a forecast: if traffic triples, what's the expected spend difference hosted vs dedicated?
03:44 Maya: We can provision a cost model spreadsheet — we'll send a cost proforma. But rule of thumb: if you have sustained 24/7 throughput and predictable peak, Dedicated makes sense at scale — often becomes cheaper past a certain monthly token volume.
03:59 Liam: Do you support autoscaling with Dedicated? We want to handle bursts without overcommitting.
04:03 Maya: Yes — Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling policies and burst capacity options — you can set min/reserve and burst behavior.
04:10 Aisha: On Private, what are the main cost drivers? Is it the ops overhead?
04:14 Daniel: Private typically has higher base cost due to packaging, private control plane, and possibly licenses for an on-prem deployment. But it gives you the most control for KMS/HSM integrations and data residency. For unit economics, if you self-manage GPUs, you control utilization which is the main lever for cost; low utilization kills unit cost.
04:32 Liam: Do you have customers that run hybrid — like hosting model in Redwood hosted for eval and move to Dedicated later?
04:37 Maya: Yeah that’s common — start on Hosted for proofs, move to Dedicated for predictable traffic, and Private only for regulated or residency needs. The API is consistent across them so code changes are minimal.
04:48 Noah: Can we run a short benchmark with our prompts? We want to measure tokens, p95 latency, and cost per 1k calls under typical concurrency.
04:56 Daniel: Absolutely. Typical pilot is a two-week bench: you share a representative prompt set, we run it on a hosted trial and on a Dedicated baseline (or our dedicated infer cluster) to show the delta. We'll also surface batching efficiency, wasted tokens, and cache hit rates.
05:10 Liam: How do I share the test set — any PII concerns?
05:13 Maya: Please sanitize sensitive PII; if you need to test with real data, Private or Dedicated with VPC+KMS is recommended. We also sign standard NDA and can do SOC 2 addenda.
05:23 Aisha: Security — quick question: do you support BYOK with HSM? We have strict KMS requirements.
05:29 Daniel: Yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations; Dedicated also supports KMS integration depending on the deployment. We'll share the security pack.
05:39 Noah: Also want to see the cost model assumptions — what granularity? monthly token forecast or per-call?
05:45 Maya: We'll send a workbook that breaks down per-token rates, effective cost after batching/caching, and projected monthly spend under different growth scenarios.
05:54 Liam: On the batching side, how much does concurrency impact latency? If you increase batch size to get cheaper per-token, does p95 blow up?
06:01 Daniel: There's a tradeoff. Our runtime uses latency SLOs to control batching: short-tail requests can bypass large batch windows; but when you have sustained concurrency, batching efficiency goes up without harming p50 — p95 can be impacted if you allow large batch windows. We expose batch timeout and max batch size per route and can set policies per SLA.
06:21 Aisha: Any caveats when using streaming for lower latency?
06:25 Daniel: Streaming slightly impacts batching because we want to deliver tokens early; the runtime can still batch initial token computation and then stream subsequent tokens. So you typically see minor differences.
06:34 Liam: Are there hidden costs — logging, observability retention charges?
06:38 Maya: Observability can be add-on. Console usage and raw transcript retention beyond default windows often have separate charges; we'll call that out in the workbook.
06:46 Noah: For forecasting, we want best/worst case per-token after optimizations — do you have typical cache hit rates?
06:51 Daniel: It depends — for templated prompts we see 20-50% effective token reduction; for research Q&A less. We'll calculate a conservative 15% and aggressive 40% scenarios in the model.
07:04 Liam: Ok, timeline: we're trying to decide by end of quarter to onboard for a pilot. Who needs to be involved from your side?
07:11 Maya: AE + SE for setup and bench; solutions can help with SSO/SAML and security docs. Post-pilot, an engagement lead for Dedicated sizing if you go that route.
07:20 Aisha: About SSO and SAML — any out-of-the-box support for role-based access? Our infra team needs RBAC.
07:26 Daniel: Yes, RBAC and SAML/SCIM provisioning are supported for both Hosted and Dedicated. For Private on-prem we can integrate with your IdP.
07:35 Liam: Any competitors we should be aware of?
07:37 Noah: We're also talking to a couple folks — Anthra? (mis-said) and a self-host vendor.
07:41 Maya: OK, we'll make sure to show where Redwood wins on unit economics and observability.
07:46 Liam: On benchmarking, can you include model variants? We want to compare LLaMA-like open models vs a few optimized quantized variants.
07:53 Daniel: Yes — we'll include open model variants, quantized 4-bit/8-bit runs, and one higher-quality baseline to show quality vs cost. We'll also surface throughput numbers (tokens/sec) for the GPUs used.
08:06 Aisha: For Dedicated pricing, is there a minimum commit?
08:09 Maya: There are commit tiers; we'll outline them. Minimums exist for monthly reserved capacity but we can propose a pilot-friendly starter.
08:18 Noah: For finance we want a simple metric: $/1k effective user-facing calls after caching and batching.
08:23 Maya: We can deliver that. We'll show a per-scenario $/1k after optimizations.
08:28 Liam: Do you do any auto-quantization suggestions? Redwood Optimize or something?
08:32 Daniel: We have Redwood Optimize that suggests batching, quantization profiles, and caching configs based on workloads. We'll run the optimizer over your sample set in the pilot.
08:42 Aisha: Any paperwork up-front? We need an NDA and security questionnaire for procurement.
08:46 Maya: We'll send the NDA and the security pack after the call.
08:49 Noah: Good. For the pilot, timeline and responsibilities?
08:52 Maya: Proposed: you share sanitized prompt set and expected concurrency by EoW; we run a two-week bench next week; deliver cost workbook + bench report within three weeks.
08:59 Liam: That works.
09:01 Maya: Ok, quick recap and next steps.
09:04 Maya: Action items: we'll send NDA + security pack; send cost workbook and pilot proposal; set up a short onboarding call for bench.
09:12 Aisha: I will extract a 500-sample prompt set and remove PII by Friday.
09:17 Noah: I'll review the cost model when you send.
09:20 Daniel: We'll provision a small test cluster and run your set, track token counts, batch utilization, and p95 latency.
09:27 Liam: Cool. Anything else?
09:29 Maya: Competitors mentioned — self-host and a vendor misnamed Anthra — we'll include comparable numbers.
09:36 Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with an email and the workbook.
09:40 Liam: Thanks folks.
09:42 [call ends]
summary: Discovery focused on cost/unit economics for Newgate Capital's deal desk assistant. Discussed per-token pricing, batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization tradeoffs, hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments, and pilot benchmarking. Next steps: NDA/security docs, share prompt set, run two-week bench, deliver cost workbook and bench report.
